clinical_category: Epilepsy self-management referral - community and group support resources
blueprint_topic: Referral to evidence-based self-management and psychosocial resources
stem: A nurse is planning discharge teaching for a client living with epilepsy who reports stress, stigma, and difficulty managing the condition day to day. Which referral is appropriate in addition to ongoing medical care?

options.A: An epilepsy self-management program or support resource that teaches coping, decision-making, and skills for living with epilepsy
options.B: A peer or self-management program used instead of prescribed antiseizure medication and clinical follow-up
options.C: No additional support, because stress, isolation, and self-management difficulties are not recognized concerns in epilepsy
options.D: A program only if seizures are uncontrolled, because self-management resources have no role for other people with epilepsy

rationale: A is correct. Current CDC epilepsy guidance states that self-management programs can help people learn skills and strategies to make good health decisions and feel better while living with epilepsy. CDC-funded programs address challenges including stress, stigma, isolation, mental health, treatment management, and use of available resources; some programs are available through group, telephone, or online formats. These resources complement—not replace—prescribed treatment and professional follow-up. B incorrectly substitutes supportive care for medical treatment. C denies problems explicitly recognized by CDC. D adds an unsupported severity restriction.
educational_objective: Connect clients with epilepsy to evidence-based self-management and support resources that build coping and disease-management skills while continuing prescribed medical care and follow-up.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_document_title: Managing Epilepsy; Managing Epilepsy Well Network
source_version_date: CDC pages dated 2024-05-15 and current at access 2026-08-18
source_locator: CDC 'Managing Epilepsy' → 'Resources and support' → self-management programs help people make good decisions about health and feel better while living with epilepsy; CDC-funded programs include group/phone/online options and programs addressing stress, stigma, isolation, depression, cognition, and self-management. CDC 'Managing Epilepsy Well Network' → Overview: self-management programs develop strategies and skills for medication/appointment management, provider communication, stress and mental-health challenges, stigma, fatigue, and finding resources.
source_claim_supported: Current CDC guidance directly supports referral to epilepsy self-management resources for coping, health decision-making, psychosocial challenges, and day-to-day disease management as an adjunct to ongoing professional care.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Management of Care client-needs subcategory (15–21% of items); includes referrals, continuity of care, client education, and coordination of community resources.
correction_summary: Substantive rebuild. The original secondary support-group source made broad claims about peer benefit across all severity levels. The final item uses current CDC epilepsy self-management resources and tests an evidence-supported referral for coping, stigma, isolation, and chronic-condition management without claiming that one support-group format is universally effective.
audit_findings: The original Epilepsy Foundation source was secondary and the item overgeneralized the benefits of generic support groups.
Current CDC guidance directly supports epilepsy self-management programs and identifies stress, stigma, isolation, mental-health needs, treatment management, and resource use as relevant targets.
The final construct treats these resources as complementary to medical care and does not imply that peer support replaces antiseizure therapy or clinical follow-up.
No unsupported disease-severity threshold or universal program-effect size is asserted.
Independent adversarial second pass found one uniquely correct answer, no second defensible option, no cueing, and no unresolved conflict.
